In my opinion, giving yourself over to ID politics is no different than buying into a fundamental religious belief system. It becomes personal, and people are lousy at critically analyzing the things that they take personally. More troubling, it leads to groupthink, and makes it easier for you to overlook the faults in your particular ideology's belief structure.

It's all good and well, for example, to say homosexuals and transsexuals should not have their rights infringed upon simply because of these two identities, but as we've seen with the fanatic wing of Left Spectrum Politics, this can absolutely go too far. Now we're treating them like a protected class, institutionalizing courses and classes on educating ridiculously young children on gender and sexuality. They don't even know what sex is, but because we've allowed sexuality to become so firmly tied to politics, we're trying to push complex ideas on children to make sure no one in this protected class are ever treated poorly by their peers.

Where the ID part of it comes into play is that now you cannot criticize this behavior in public discourse without being labeled a bigot, without being shoved into another Spectrum of ID politics that you would not normally associate with.

At the end of the day, ID Politics makes proper debate and discussion all but impossible, because it removes the topics of discussion from the realm of critical analysis, and ties them to individuals on a deeply personal level, so that they cannot help but feel assaulted when you critique the topic. Then their emotional attachment gets involved, and it becomes a bitch fest instead of a debate.

ID Politics play a relevant role raising issues, but it creates new issues when it becomes the driver in policy making. Nowadays they got in control of the policy making due to the lack of vision and spine in the Left. The Left has been hijacked due to its weakness

The Left needs to find itself, not by contrast to the right, but with clear principles and beliefs. And those should come from a equalitarian, and humanistic perspective. So the same left should not entertain policies that discriminate, not even positively (some will argue that's needed to compensate and change course and reach the desired balance, but I would argue that those measures should always be limited in time).

ID Politics do not make debate and discussion impossible. It enriches it if it is just taken into consideration, and not given central stage attention. ID politics supporters need to understand that their role is not to create the policy but to make sure it does not harm their group or any other, including the majority of people that are not part of their group.

One of the problems with ID politics is that it is so reductionist about identity. While there are differences between many groups, the actual number of groups is huge, and it's usually reduced to a few mostly arbitrary differences that are amplified for political advantage. Like the ole' "one drop rule". The two groups of people I've seen actively promoting this the most are one; University professors and students, and two; hard right white nationalists.

If I wanted to be really accurate, I'd need to identify every single group a person fits into, from stuff like "male" and "asian", to "people who were abused by meth addicted parents" all the way to stuff like "people who briefly paused while brushing their teeth at 8:13 this morning". Either that, or abandon the concept of identity groups altogether.

Group assignment can be a useful mental shortcut in some cases, for example, when examining the perceptions people have of other groups. Humans are generally very good at identifying and matching patterns, and group assignment leverages that. But unless one takes the time to keep in mind how limited the value of most group assignments is, it will distort our thinking more than if we rejected it, IMO. All too often, IDPol is just another layer that creates arguments, and needs to be worked around before actual work can begin.

Personally I think that the counter part of ID Politics falls in two possibilities: One is opposing it, treating it as a threat that has no benefit and has to be fought. This is the approach of the Establishment and anybody that benefits of the current status quo that ID Politics challenge. The other approach is a more productive one, a Equalitarian and humanistic approach. In this case the input from IDPolitics is taken into account as relevant input, but the principle of equality prevents from introducing positive discrimination policies, and instead ensures that no discrimination is facilitated/endorsed/tolerated by the society.

Obviously those supporting ID Politics want a larger influence and power, as the positive discrimination policies provide. Personally I am more for a humanistic approach, where they can be considered just as any other actor of society, but should not drive the policy making. Equality, no discrimination and human rights should.
